claims.text: A cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type eutectic high-entropy alloy forms dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
The as-cast baseline has limited room-temperature tensile ductility because microcracks initiate along lamellar interfaces.
Adding less than approximately 0.1 wt% interstitial carbon during synthesis will produce nanoscale coherent carbides or carbon-rich particles preferentially at lamellar interfaces.
Keeping carbon below approximately 0.1 wt% will avoid coarse, brittle carbide formation.
Fine interfacial carbides will improve phase-boundary cohesion and impede microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Interfacial carbide precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion and provide precipitation/dislocation strengthening.
Phase-boundary structures in dual-phase HEAs can influence dislocation behavior.
Carbide-induced dislocation pinning will enhance progressive strain hardening and delay tensile failure.
The carbon-modified alloy will have higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified lamellar alloy at room temperature.
The carbon-modified alloy will have greater total room-temperature tensile elongation than the unmodified lamellar alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will show improved strain hardening and delayed microcrack formation at lamellar interfaces.
Dual-phase HEAs designed using second-phase strengthening can combine high strength with room-temperature tensile ductility.
Coarse, inhomogeneous, or non-coherent carbides can cause earlier crack initiation and embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-cast alloy, but the conditions and experiment describe both test and control alloys as receiving casting plus controlled thermo-mechanical processing. Thus, the proposed experimental control is not necessarily the stated as-cast baseline.
